To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
BCI performance is related to the ability of a subject to observe movements.

(i) high aptitude BCI-users show higher activation in the SMA during observation of movements than low aptitude BSI users and that (ii) BCI performance in high aptitude BSI-users is significantly correlated with the number of activated areas in the right middle front gyrus during observation of movements.

the ability to regulate brain and behavior through learning mechanisms involving motor imagery such as required for controlling a brain-computer interface is tightly related to recall of sensorimotor programs reflected in the electroencecephalogram during observation of movement sequences and unrelated to the motor execution of these movements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural correlates of BCI-control, which is a novel approach to investigate the neural correlates of motor imagery and observation.
the neural mechanisms underlying the ability to control a BBI.
understanding the neural correlates of BCI-control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ability to control a B CI depends on the activation of the SMA during the observation of movement and is related to the ability of the user to recall the sensorimotor program during BCI control.
motor imagery and movement observation are closely linked to BCI-control.

the ability to regulate behavior through imagery is the consequence of 1) a sensorimotor learning process that is reflected by the acquisition of a sensor-motor program in the EEG during motor imagery, 2) the recall of such a sensorimotor programs through motor observation and 3) the ability to monitor the execution of the task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural correlates of BCI-control reflect the ability to recall and regulate behavior through the activation of motor brain systems.
BCI-control is a consequence of a sensorimotory representation of movements and the ability to recall such representations during observation of movement.
BCI performance is related to the activation of motor brain areas during the observation of movements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ability to control an SMR-BCIs is not related to the ability to execute the motor sequences, but rather to the recall of the sensorimotor programs associated with these motor sequences.
BCI-control can be learned by observation of movement.
motor imagery can be used as a tool to train the brain to generate a specific cortical activation pattern that can be detected by an EEG-BCI.
